judgments.reasoning_cat1: The listing of named coverages plus the condition that underlying insurance "afford limits not less than" the Schedule leaves open how a policy with differing or self-insured underlying limits is treated, and "excess liability policies" is not defined. The enumerated coverage list also invites expressio unius arguments about coverages not named.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: This paragraph was wholly replaced by Amendment No. 4 for policies effective on or after October 1, 1996, and it must be read against Article III's treatment of self-insured underlying Hospital Professional Liability limits, which contemplates the absence of the underlying insurance this Article requires.
judgments.clause_name: Article I — APPLICATION OF AGREEMENT (Reinsurance Agreement)

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The schedule is a set of numeric limits with defined bases (each occurrence, each medical incident, annual aggregate) and little interpretive play. "Combined single limit" and the aircraft sub-items are conventional insurance terms.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Amendment No. 4 adds entries to this schedule that duplicate outpatient facility limits, and Article III's self-insured proviso assumes the scheduled underlying limit may not exist as insurance, creating some friction with the schedule's premise.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The sentence both folds the discovery period into the policy period and then says "a separate Limit of liability may apply in respect thereof" — "may" leaves it uncertain whether a separate limit applies automatically, at the reinsured's option, or only if the underlying policy so provides. That is a genuine ambiguity about aggregation of limits.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It interacts with Article III's per-occurrence/annual aggregate caps and with Article XI's run-off of discovery period coverages after cancellation, so the number of available limits in the run-off period is contestable.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A short incorporation-by-attachment sentence with no operative discretion or vague term. Its meaning is plain.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The attached Nuclear Incident Exclusion Clause No. 1 addresses physical damage, which sits oddly in a liability reinsurance treaty, but incorporation itself is consistent with the instrument.
judgments.clause_name: Incorporation of Nuclear Incident Exclusion and Insolvency Clauses

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "Teaching hospital," "children's hospital" and "psychiatric hospital" are undefined classifications that many hospitals partially satisfy, and "loss arising out of the operation by the insured of" a teaching hospital is a further vague causal link. Whether a general hospital with residency programs is a "teaching hospital" is a classic construction fight.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Article I's Rating Schedule expressly rates employed interns, residents and physicians and occupied psychiatric beds, which is hard to reconcile with an exclusion of teaching and psychiatric hospital operations; Amendment No. 1 narrows the exclusion only prospectively.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The provision supplies its own definition of "total beds," but the definition qualifies only acute care beds as "occupied" while listing the remaining categories unqualified, so the count basis is internally uncertain. The 250 threshold itself is definite.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The same categories reappear in the Rating Schedule as "occupied bed equivalents," which uses "occupied" throughout and applies weights, so the two counting conventions do not line up; Amendment No. 1 raises the figure to 350 prospectively.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "Ownership, operation or use of helicopters owned or leased by the insured hospital" is concrete and self-limiting. Little room for competing readings.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Article I affirmatively brings Heliport Liability and Non-Owned Aircraft Liability within the treaty, so the boundary between covered heliport operations and excluded owned/leased helicopter operations must be harmonised.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A closed list of named counties with no catch-all; application is mechanical once a risk's location is known. Punctuation is slightly loose but the counties are identifiable.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Amendment No. 1 replaces this list and drops Cuyahoga County, while Rating Schedule-A then rates Cleveland in Territory 3, which is coherent rather than conflicting.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: After enumerating pool, syndicate, association, insolvency fund and guaranty fund, the clause adds "or other combination of insurers or reinsurers formed for the purpose of" covering specified coverages or geographies — a catch-all of uncertain reach against the specifics. Whether a fronting or facultative arrangement is such a "combination" is arguable.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It overlaps the attached Nuclear Incident Exclusion Clauses' pool exclusions and exclusion (f) for assumed reinsurance, but the overlap is cumulative rather than contradictory.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "Reinsurance assumed by the REINSURED" is a term of art with a settled meaning in the industry. The wording is short and definite.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Consistent with Article I's focus on the reinsured's own excess liability policies and with the Offset article's reference to other treaties.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "Business to the extent that it is reinsured outside of this agreement" is open-ended: it does not say whether facultative, quota-share or other treaty reinsurance triggers it, nor how "to the extent" apportions a partially reinsured risk. That phrase carries real interpretive risk.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It sits against the Offset article, which contemplates other reinsurance agreements between the same parties, and against Article III's self-insured retention mechanics, so its bite on layered programmes is contestable.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The text states "$9,000,000 of loss each occurrence/$93,000,000 annual aggregate," an evident numerical error against the $10,000,000 aggregate cap and the $9,000,000 excess layer just described. The self-insured proviso is also a single run-on sentence whose 90%/10% split is easy to misread.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is superseded twice — by Amendment No. 1 ($25,000,000) and Amendment No. 4 (with a $10,000,000 sub-limit for nursing home and outpatient business) — so which limit governs a given policy year turns on the amendments' effective-date language.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The definition is exhaustive ("shall mean only") yet includes prejudgment interest within loss while the companion definition of claim expenses includes "interest upon judgments," and paragraphs (b) and (c) cover extracontractual and punitive exposure at 90% subject to the vague precondition that the Corporation "counseled with" and "concurred in" the reinsured's course of conduct. Those phrases are prime candidates for dispute.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It must be reconciled with Article V's proportional indemnity for claim expenses and with the Insolvency Clause proviso, and the exclusion of statutory penalties in the following paragraph sits uneasily with paragraph (c)'s coverage of punitive and exemplary damages.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The recovery-sharing formula is expressed as a counterfactual reconstruction ("what it would have been had the recovery preceded any payment"), which is workable but requires computation rather than construction. "After expenses" is undefined but conventional.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The Accounting Schedule separately credits to profits "all salvage received by the CORPORATION," so the same recovery is handled in two places and their interaction must be harmonised.
judgments.clause_name: ARTICLE IV. Salvage and Subrogation Recovery

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "All payments under the supplementary payments provisions of the REINSURED'S policy, including court costs, interest upon judgments, and allocated investigation, adjustment, and legal expenses" is a general phrase followed by specifics, leaving the reach of unlisted items (e.g. unallocated or in-house costs) uncertain. "Interest upon judgments" also overlaps the prejudgment interest included in loss.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It directly abuts the definition of loss, which includes prejudgment interest subject to the policy limit, and Article V allocates claim expenses proportionally, so classification of interest determines whether the limit applies.
judgments.clause_name: Article IV — Definition of "claim expenses" (Reinsurance Agreement)

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Two short, concrete carve-outs — employee salaries and statutory unfair-practice penalties. The wording is definite.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The penalty carve-out is in tension with the loss definition's paragraph (c), which shares punitive, exemplary and compensatory damages arising from claims-handling conduct at 90%.
judgments.clause_name: ARTICLE IV. Exclusions from Loss and Claim Expenses

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The proviso speaks of expenses "connected with such settlement or appeal" although only a verdict, award or judgment reduced or reversed on appeal has been described, and "total benefit resulting from such reduction or reversal" is not defined. Both are genuine sources of argument about the ratio to be applied.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It depends on the definitions of loss and claim expenses in Article IV, whose treatment of interest and extracontractual amounts changes the denominator "total amount of loss."
judgments.clause_name: Article V — INDEMNITY FOR CLAIM EXPENSES (Reinsurance Agreement)

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A straightforward obligation keyed to an attached Rating Schedule and stated minimum premiums. No vague operative term.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The Rating Schedule is replaced twice (Schedule-A, then Schedule-B) and Amendment No. 2 edits Territory 1, so the applicable schedule for a given policy depends on the amendments' effective dates.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A single fixed percentage ceding commission; the only defect is OCR noise in the word "ceding." Meaning is plain.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Consistent with the Accounting Schedule, which credits written premium "net after ceding commission," so the two provisions dovetail.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Substantial portions of the operative first sentence and of the accounting-period proviso are illegible, and what remains combines "a new accounting period shall commence on January 1st of every other year" with a final period beginning on "the fifth January 1st preceding the termination date," which cannot be reconciled with a twenty-four month period. The mechanics as written are internally inconsistent.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Amendment No. 1 replaces this first paragraph and caps the commission at the first $1,000,000 of limits, while the Accounting Schedule computes profit on all premium and losses, and the Stipulation of Termination supplies no "termination date" of the kind this article presupposes.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The item numbering is broken (an unnumbered second credit, a stray "4a."), and the overhead charge is keyed to "Item i of Credits to Profits" whose identity depends on that numbering. Losses are also charged on an "attributable to claims occurring or claims made (depending on policy coverage)" basis that is left to inference.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Read with Amendment No. 1's limitation of contingent commission to the first $1,000,000 of reinsured limits, the schedule's whole-account premium and loss items no longer match the commission base.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "Calculated on the reserve of individual cases as developed to the date the computation is made" leaves who sets the case reserves, and on what basis, unstated. That is a modest but real vagueness in a figure that drives the commission.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It works with the Accounting Schedule's charge for unpaid losses and the Inspection of Records article, and no contrary provision appears.
judgments.clause_name: ARTICLE VII. Definition of Unpaid Losses

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A plain arithmetic definition of deficit with a carry-forward instruction. No ambiguous term.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It duplicates Accounting Schedule charge item 4 (prior period deficit), which is reinforcing rather than conflicting.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A one-line arithmetic definition, the mirror image of the deficit definition. Nothing to construe in the words.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Amendment No. 1 pays 40% of "net profit accruing to the REINSURED" but only as respects the first $1,000,000 of limits, whereas net profit here is defined across the whole account, leaving the base for the calculation unsettled.
judgments.clause_name: ARTICLE VII. Definition of Net Profit

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The opening words are garbled, and as best read the clause bars any accounting period commencing on or after the termination date while deferring further commission until all premium is earned and all losses paid — two distinct rules whose relationship to the deferred computation cycle is unclear. The uncertainty is in the timing mechanism itself.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The Stipulation of Termination terminates only "with respect to loss under policies issued on or after January 1, 1998" and states no termination date, and Article XI's run-off extends coverage for up to twelve months plus odd time, so the trigger for this clause is contestable.
judgments.clause_name: ARTICLE VII. No Accounting Period After Termination

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Two short deadlines and a bordereau requirement "on a form satisfactory to the CORPORATION," which is a discretionary but conventional standard. Otherwise definite.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It complements the Offset article and Article IX's loss reimbursement mechanics without contradicting them.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "Prompt notice" of "any event or development which might result in a claim" is an open-textured trigger, and the scope of documents to be forwarded is limited to those "requested by the CORPORATION." Late-notice disputes turn precisely on such wording.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is echoed by the Insolvency Clause, which preserves the ceding company's duty to investigate, settle and defend, and by the Corporation's joint-participation right; the provisions align.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The right is expressly conditioned on "the judgment of the CORPORATION," which forecloses argument about the trigger, and it is a right rather than a duty. Wording is definite.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It sits comfortably beside Article IX's allocation of the defence to the reinsured and the Insolvency Clause's parallel right to interpose defences at the reinsurer's own expense.
judgments.clause_name: Article IX — CLAIMS: Corporation's right of joint participation

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Reimbursement is conditioned on receipt of "satisfactory evidence of payment of such loss," a standard whose sufficiency is judged by the payer and is a familiar point of contention. "Promptly" is likewise undefined.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The immediately following paragraph obliges the Corporation to fund on the date the reinsured proposes to pay, which cuts against a precondition of proof of payment already made.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The sentence is mangled — "will furnish to the REINSURED the CORPORATION'S Payment of loss ... on the same date on which the REINSURED proposes to make payment" — leaving the mechanism and any notice period unstated. As written it is barely operative.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is in tension with the preceding paragraph's requirement of satisfactory evidence of payment before reimbursement, since funding in advance necessarily precedes such evidence.
judgments.clause_name: ARTICLE IX. Advance Funding of Loss Payment

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A one-sentence access right limited to "records ... pertaining to the risks reinsured hereunder." Broad but not ambiguous in any nameable respect.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It supports the Accounting Schedule's reserve-based computations and the bordereau reporting obligation; nothing contradicts it.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The right extends to balances under "any other reinsurance agreement heretofore or hereafter entered into," which is broad, but the categories offset (premiums, commissions, loss, claim expenses) are enumerated and clear. Reciprocity is expressly stated.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Its reference to other treaties between the same parties runs alongside exclusion (g) for business reinsured outside this agreement, but the two operate on different subjects.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "Twelve months plus odd time" is industry shorthand whose boundary is not defined in the agreement, and the run-off sentence combines natural expiration, next anniversary and a twelve-month cap in a way that requires reconciling. The discovery-period sentence adds coverages attaching "prior to or as of the effective date in time of cancellation."
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The Stipulation of Termination terminates the treaty by reference to policies issued on or after January 1, 1998 rather than by the 90-day notice and run-off mechanism prescribed here, and Article VII's contingent commission depends on a "termination date" this clause defines differently.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Standard market wording excluding liability accruing from any nuclear pool, "directly or indirectly and whether as insurer or reinsurer." The formula is well worn and definite.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It overlaps Article II exclusion (e) for pool participation, which is cumulative rather than inconsistent.
judgments.clause_name: Nuclear Incident Exclusion Clause No. 1 (1) - Pools

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The clause turns on undefined terms such as "critical facilities" and "substantial quantities" of radioactive isotopes, though a later paragraph makes the reinsured sole judge of the latter. OCR damage aside, it is boilerplate.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: This is a physical damage exclusion attached to a liability-only excess treaty covering the coverages listed in Article I, so much of it can have no application; that is redundancy rather than contradiction.
judgments.clause_name: Nuclear Incident Exclusion Clause No. 1 (2) - Physical Damage

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The carve-outs for lack of knowledge and for policies containing a radioactive contamination exclusion depend on "knowledge" and on governmental approval dates, but these are conventional market terms. Text is heavily degraded rather than substantively ambiguous.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Consistent with the other nuclear paragraphs and with the incorporation sentence in Article I.
judgments.clause_name: Nuclear Incident Exclusion Clause No. 1 (3) - Radioactive Contamination

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "When such radioactive contamination is a named hazard specifically insured against" is a narrow, testable condition. Little interpretive latitude.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It coheres with the preceding paragraphs of the same clause and with nothing else in the treaty.
judgments.clause_name: Nuclear Incident Exclusion Clause No. 1 (4) - Named Hazard

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The exception depends on whether the nuclear exposure is "the primary hazard," a judgment expressly committed to the reinsured, and the paragraph as reproduced runs together with the sole-judge and special-material definitions. The primary-hazard test is inherently imprecise even with the sole-judge allocation.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is internally consistent with the rest of the nuclear clause and with the Corporation's audit and inspection rights.
judgments.clause_name: Nuclear Incident Exclusion Clause No. 1 (5) - Non-Primary Hazard

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A definition by cross-reference to the Atomic Energy Act of 1954 "or by any law amendatory thereof," which is external but determinate. No competing reading is available.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Fits the surrounding nuclear paragraphs that use the defined term.
judgments.clause_name: Nuclear Incident Exclusion Clause No. 1 (6) - Special Nuclear Material

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The clause makes the reinsured sole judge of "substantial quantities" and of "the extent of installation, plant or site," which removes the ambiguity by allocating the decision but leaves the good-faith limits of that discretion open. Terms themselves remain vague on their face.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: No other provision purports to allocate that judgment differently; it is consistent with the whole.
judgments.clause_name: Nuclear Incident Exclusion Clause No. 1 (7) - Reinsured Sole Judge

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A grandfathering rule tied to policies issued on or before 31 December 1957 with an expiry-or-date-whichever-first-occurs test. Mechanical and dated but not ambiguous.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Given the 1994 effective date this paragraph can have no practical application, which is obsolescence rather than incoherence.
judgments.clause_name: Nuclear Incident Exclusion Clause No. 1 (8) - Policies Issued Before 1957

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A parallel grandfathering rule for Canadian risks, similarly date-driven. The operative test is clear on its face.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Consistent with the preceding grandfathering paragraph; nothing in the treaty contradicts it.
judgments.clause_name: Nuclear Incident Exclusion Clause No. 1 (9) - Canadian Risks

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Standard association/subscriber exclusion, with "direct or indirect reinsurer of any such member" spelled out. Definite market language.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It duplicates Article II exclusion (e) in substance, which is cumulative and creates no operative conflict.
judgments.clause_name: Nuclear Incident Exclusion Clause No. 2 (1) - Association Membership

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The Limited Exclusion Provision applies only to enumerated personal-lines policy classes and "policies of a similar nature," an ejusdem generis catch-all whose reach is uncertain, and the text is further obscured by OCR loss. The classes listed have no obvious relation to hospital excess liability.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Article I limits the treaty to commercial hospital-related coverages, so this personal-lines machinery has no field of operation; redundancy rather than contradiction.
judgments.clause_name: Nuclear Incident Exclusion Clause No. 2 (2) - Limited Exclusion Provision

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The Broad Exclusion Provision applies to a long enumerated list of liability coverages, and although the list includes Professional and Malpractice Liability, the closing reference to a clause "V" not reproduced leaves the deeming time unstated. The list-plus-cross-reference structure is the weak point.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The coverages listed overlap Article I's covered coverages, so the interaction between the deemed nuclear exclusion and the reinsured's actual policy wordings must be worked out, though no direct conflict appears.
judgments.clause_name: Nuclear Incident Exclusion Clause No. 2 (3) - Broad Exclusion Provision

judgments.reasoning_cat1: This is the statutory-form insolvency clause; its terms (payment without diminution, payee exceptions, evidentiary effect of judgments) are prescribed and well settled. The reference to "Section 4118 of the Insurance Law of New York" in an Ohio treaty is odd but determinate.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Article IV's proviso expressly defers to "the provisions of the insolvency clause of this agreement," so the two dovetail.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The paragraph preserves the ceding company's claim-handling duties and gives the reinsurer a defence right at its own expense, with expense sharing "subject to court approval" and proportionate to benefit. "Reasonable time" for notice is the only soft term.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It mirrors Article IX's allocation of investigation and defence and the Corporation's joint-participation right, and is consistent with them.
judgments.clause_name: Insolvency Clause - Obligations of Ceding Company and Reinsurer's Defense

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "A majority in interest" is undefined, and apportionment "in accordance with the terms of this reinsurance agreement as though such expense had been incurred by the ceding insurer" is somewhat circular in a treaty whose expense provision is Article V's proportional formula. The mechanism is workable but not self-evident.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It requires reading with Article V's claim-expense ratio, which is keyed to loss borne by the Corporation; the cross-reference functions without contradiction.
judgments.clause_name: Insolvency Clause - Two or More Reinsurers

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A savings clause preserving the ceding-insurer/reinsurer relationship and disclaiming third-party rights, with express exceptions. Its wording is dense but definite.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Consistent with the rest of the insolvency clause and with Article IV's insolvency proviso.
judgments.clause_name: Insolvency Clause - No Change in Relationship

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The definitional sentence is jumbled so that "Occupied Bed Equivalents" is separated from its definition, and item 9 assigns CRNAs a range of "x 5-10" with no rule for choosing within the range. That open factor directly affects premium.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The bed categories here differ in weighting from the flat "total beds" count used in Article II exclusion (b), but the two serve different functions and can be harmonised.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The territory definition is scrambled in reproduction, with the state list and the Territory 2 cities interleaved, and Akron appears among the cities while only two multipliers are given. Whether Akron carries the 1.50 multiplier is not clearly answered.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Rating Schedule-A and Amendment No. 2 replace these territories entirely, and Cleveland's absence here contrasts with Cuyahoga County's exclusion in Article II(d), which is coherent.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The amendment is stated "Effective January 1, 1904," an obvious mis-typing of 1994, and the proviso that "this article shall apply only to the first $1,000,000 of reinsured limits as respects each policy" does not say how premium, losses and expenses are to be split between that layer and the rest. Both the date error and the untold allocation rule are nameable defects.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The retained Accounting Schedule computes net profit on all written premium and all paid and unpaid losses without any layer split, so the amended commission base cannot be derived from the surviving machinery.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The substituted exclusion turns wholly on the undefined phrase "teaching hospital," now without even the "by the insured" qualifier, and the clause ends with a comma suggesting truncation. Whether a hospital with affiliated residency programmes is excluded is exactly the kind of question that is litigated.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The Rating Schedules expressly rate employed interns, residents and physicians, which implies teaching activity is contemplated within the covered book, creating tension with a blanket teaching-hospital exclusion.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The 350-bed threshold is numeric and the definition of "total beds" is supplied, although as in the original only acute care beds are qualified as "occupied." That inconsistency in the definition persists.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It applies only to policies effective on or after July 1, 1995, leaving the 250-bed original in force for earlier policies, which is orderly rather than incoherent.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A closed list of six named counties with no catch-all; application is mechanical. Wording is definite.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Rating Schedule-A's Territory 2 entry for Michigan reads "All areas except Wayne and Oakland County," which dovetails with this exclusion rather than conflicting with it.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The limits are stated cleanly, but the self-insured proviso remains a single run-on sentence combining a 90% retention, a 10% share and a $24,000,000 excess layer. The temporal reach of the substitution — whether it touches policies written before July 1, 1995 — is not stated in the substituted text itself.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It deletes the original Article III and is in turn deleted by Amendment No. 4, which adds a $10,000,000 sub-limit for nursing home and outpatient business, so the operative limit for any given policy depends on layered effective dates.
judgments.clause_name: Article III — RETENTION AND REINSURANCE (as substituted by Amendment No. 1)

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A simple deletion-and-substitution instruction naming the replaced and replacing schedules. Nothing to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Amendment No. 2 then amends Schedule-A and Amendment No. 4 replaces it with Schedule-B, a clean chain of substitutions.
judgments.clause_name: Amendment No. 1, III. Substitution of Rating Schedule-A

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "In all other respects not inconsistent herewith" makes the survival of original terms depend on the undefined notion of inconsistency, which is precisely the question a dispute would present. The qualifier is doing real work here.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Applied to this amendment it must decide, for example, whether the Accounting Schedule survives unchanged alongside the new $1,000,000 commission cap and whether the original Article II(a) survives for pre-July 1995 policies.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The list of weights is legible, but the CRNA factor is again "x 5-10" with no selection rule, and the item numbering is garbled in reproduction. The open range is the identifiable defect.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It parallels the original Rating Schedule and Schedule-B without substantive divergence.
judgments.clause_name: Rating Schedule-A - Hospital Rating Occupied Bed Equivalents

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Territory 1 is defined residually as "the remainder of the states ... not listed in Territories 2 or 3," and Territory 2 entries such as "Seattle & Tacoma Metro areas" and "All areas except Wayne and Oakland County" have soft boundaries. "Metro areas" is a nameable vagueness.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Amendment No. 2 adds Iowa and South Dakota to this Territory 1, but Rating Schedule-B then drops Iowa, South Dakota and Washington from Territory 1 while also dropping the Washington and Michigan entries from Territory 2, leaving accounts in those states unrated.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Two concrete entries, Cleveland and "All cities" in Alaska. Definite on its face.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Cleveland's inclusion is consistent with Amendment No. 1's deletion of the Cuyahoga County exclusion, so the rating and exclusion provisions cohere.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Three numeric multipliers matched to three territories. No interpretive question.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Fits the territory definitions immediately preceding, subject only to the state-coverage gap created later by Schedule-B.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The heading is destroyed in reproduction so the factor ".125" floats free of any identified coverage or state, and it is unclear whether it is a multiplier or a credit. Schedule-B's corresponding entry reads "for umbrella excluding BPL," itself a probable mis-typing of PL.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Schedule-B repeats the entry with an added Wisconsin contingent endorsement charge, and neither Article I nor Article II mentions Indiana or Wisconsin contingent coverage, so the premium item lacks an operative counterpart.
judgments.clause_name: Rating Schedule-A - Indiana and Wisconsin Factor

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Five year-by-year credits stated as percentages, with the fifth marked mature. Mechanically clear.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Rating Schedule-B restates these factors with different values (35% in the second year and 15% mature), which is a permitted replacement rather than a conflict.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The two credit percentages are printed above, rather than beside, the two categories of risk, so which credit attaches to which category is not stated by the text itself. That layout defect changes the premium result.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Schedule-B restates the same credits with the categories properly paired, which resolves the pairing but confirms the earlier entry's defect.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A clean substitution of a state list, with "Webraska" plainly Nebraska and the residual formula preserved. Nothing genuinely ambiguous.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Amendment No. 4's Rating Schedule-B replaces Territory 1 again and omits Iowa, South Dakota and Washington, so this amendment's additions are silently lost and Washington accounts fall outside every territory.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "Not inconsistent herewith" again leaves the survival of prior terms to an undefined inconsistency test. The rest is boilerplate.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: For this narrow territorial amendment there is little scope for inconsistency, so the qualifier does less work here than in the other amendments.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A name-change substitution with an express effective date; the only oddity is the OCR rendering of "July." Meaning is plain.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Later provisions still refer to "OHIC's discretion" and "the REINSURED," which the substitution accommodates without contradiction.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The same "not inconsistent herewith" formula, whose operation depends on an undefined test. Standard boilerplate.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Applied to a pure name change there is nothing for it to reconcile, so relational risk is slight.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The substituted paragraph introduces a "claims-conversion basis" that is nowhere defined in the agreement except by a rating factor in Schedule-B, and it adds Nursing Home and Outpatient Facility Professional Liability without defining those risks. "Outpatient facility" is a nameable open term given the later exclusions.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The added coverages must be read with Amendment No. 4's exclusions (j) and (k), which strip out surgicenters, emergicenters, hospices, laboratories and outpatient facilities with employed treating physicians, so the scope of the new grant is contestable.
judgments.clause_name: Amendment No. 4, A. Replacement First Paragraph of Article I

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The addition lists "Nursing Homes and Outpatient Facilities Professional Liability" and then, separately, "Outpatient Facility Professional Liability" with identical limits — a duplication indicating a drafting slip about whether outpatient facilities are grouped with nursing homes or stand alone. The entry also spells "Facilitiy."
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Amendment No. 4's Article III distinguishes "Nursing Home and Outpatient Facility Professional Liability" as a single class with a $10,000,000 limit, so the duplicated schedule entry does not map cleanly onto the retention article or onto Schedule-B's separate Nursing Home and Facility rating sections.
judgments.clause_name: Amendment No. 4, B. Additions to Schedule of Underlying Limits

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "More than five locations" is precise, but the saving condition — "unless the primary Commercial General Liability and Professional Liability limits apply per location" — leaves it unclear whether both limits must be per location and how partial per-location structures are treated. That condition is the soft point.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It presupposes the underlying limits added to the Schedule of Underlying Limits by the same amendment, whose duplicated outpatient entry makes the applicable primary limit for a mixed nursing home/outpatient risk uncertain.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "Fire resistive" is a construction-classification term of art not defined here, and "sprinklered" is not qualified as fully or partially. The five-story threshold itself is definite.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Nothing else in the treaty addresses building construction, so the exclusion stands alone without relational strain.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The list "surgicenters, emergicenters, hospices or laboratories" uses informal category names with no catch-all and no definitions, so a facility with mixed functions is hard to place. The absence of a general term limits, but does not remove, the difficulty.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The same amendment adds Outpatient Facility Professional Liability to Article I and a Facility Rating section to Schedule-B, and this exclusion removes much of what an outpatient facility typically is, leaving the grant and the exclusion pulling in opposite directions.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The exclusion turns on physicians "who provide patient care" and then exempts "medical directors and other administrative positions which may be staffed by a physician," a distinction that collapses where a medical director also treats patients. The carve-out's boundary is the identifiable ambiguity.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The Rating Schedules charge for employed interns, residents and physicians as part of occupied bed equivalents, which sits uneasily with excluding facilities that employ treating physicians.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The final sentence — "As respects claims made policy forms, each claim shall be deemed an occurrence hereunder" — interacts with an annual aggregate expressed per occurrence, leaving batch or multi-claimant incidents unresolved, and the sub-limit in (b) does not say how a policy mixing hospital and outpatient exposures is capped. Those are nameable tensions in the wording.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Article I's discovery-period sentence contemplates that a separate limit of liability "may apply" to extended reporting periods, which cuts against the fixed annual aggregate here, and the sub-limit must be reconciled with the duplicated underlying-limits entry added by the same amendment.
judgments.clause_name: Amendment No. 4, D. Replacement Article III Retention and Reinsurance

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A plain instruction deleting Schedule-A and substituting Schedule-B. No ambiguity.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It silently overrides Amendment No. 2's edit of Schedule-A's Territory 1, which is the source of the state-coverage gap, though the substitution instruction itself is clear.
judgments.clause_name: Amendment No. 4, E. Substitution of Rating Schedule-B

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The same undefined "not inconsistent herewith" qualifier governing survival of prior terms. Its application is a matter of judgment.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Here it must decide whether Amendment No. 2's territorial additions survive the wholesale substitution of Schedule-B and whether the original contingent commission machinery still fits the expanded book.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The weights are legible and conventional, but CRNAs are again given as "x 5-10" with no rule for selecting a figure. That range is the only real softness.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It reproduces the earlier schedules' definition without divergence and feeds the rate tables that follow.
judgments.clause_name: Rating Schedule-B - Hospital Rating Occupied Bed Equivalents

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Territory 1 is again residual ("not listed in Territories 2 or 3"), so its content depends entirely on the completeness of the other two lists. The wording is otherwise clear.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Compared with Amendment No. 2's Territory 1 and Schedule-A's Territory 2, this version drops Iowa, South Dakota and Washington from Territory 1 and drops the Michigan and Washington entries from Territory 2, so accounts in those states fall into no territory and no multiplier can be applied.
judgments.clause_name: Rating Schedule-B - Territorial Multipliers and Territories

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Two definite entries. Nothing to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Consistent with the Territory 3 multiplier and with the deletion of the Cuyahoga County exclusion by Amendment No. 1.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Three numeric multipliers matched to the three territories. Definite.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It presupposes that every account falls within one of the three territories, which the Territory 1 and 2 lists in Schedule-B do not ensure.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "Incidental owned automobile exposure" is undefined and the triggers — "Any Owned Ambulances involved in emergency runs" or "More than 10 owned automobiles" — do not say how a fleet is counted or what happens to non-owned exposure. "Incidental" is the nameable vague term.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Article I covers Automobile Liability excess of a $1,000,000 underlying limit, so a rating rule that charges nothing for incidental exposure must be reconciled with the minimum premium provisions.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The heading reads "excluding BPL," apparently a mis-typing of PL, and the Wisconsin contingent endorsement charge is given as a bare "25" without units, so it is unclear whether a factor or a percentage is meant. Both are mechanical defects that change the premium.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: No operative article of the treaty addresses a Wisconsin contingent endorsement, so the charge has no counterpart in the coverage grant of Article I.
judgments.clause_name: Rating Schedule-B - Indiana and Wisconsin Factor

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The second and third year credits are both stated as 35%, an evident error against the descending pattern and against Schedule-A's 45% second-year figure. The mistake directly affects premium calculation.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It also disturbs the Claim-Conversion factor immediately following, which is applied to the "Mature Claims-Made premium in accordance with the above schedule."

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "Apply a 1.30 factor to the Mature Claims-Made premium in accordance with the above schedule" is doubly referential, and it is unclear whether the conversion period runs from inception or from the conversion. "At no additional cost" is clear enough.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: A free extended reporting endorsement sits against Article I's provision that a separate limit of liability may apply to such endorsements and against Article XI's run-off wording, so the reinsurer's exposure for the free endorsement is not clearly priced or limited.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Two credits properly paired with two categories and expressly excluded from minimum premiums. Clear.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Consistent with the minimum premium tables that follow, which are stated not to be subject to the credits.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The first million is derived from "OHIC's Manual GL and Professional Liability Premium (before application of experience and schedule rating)," a figure fixed by the reinsured's own manual and outside the treaty, which leaves the reinsurer dependent on an undefined external base. The automobile loads are precise.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The Inspection of Records article gives access to the reinsured's records, which mitigates the external-reference problem; nothing else contradicts this rating basis.
judgments.clause_name: Rating Schedule-B - Nursing Home Rating Rates

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Schedule credit or debit "at the REINSURED'S discretion but not to exceed 25% for a credit" caps credits but leaves debits unlimited and the discretion unqualified. The asymmetry is a nameable feature rather than an ambiguity.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It must be read with the nursing home minimum premium provision, which is expressly not subject to rating credits, and with Article VI's minimum premium obligation.
judgments.clause_name: Rating Schedule-B - Nursing Home Rating Credits

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The percentages are printed as a block detached from the layer descriptions and the "Minimum Premiums:" heading is embedded in the list, so matching each factor to its million of limit depends on inference. "The next $9,000,000" is stated clearly.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Amendment No. 4's Article III caps nursing home and outpatient business at $10,000,000, which matches the first million plus the next $9,000,000, so the layers and the limits cohere.
judgments.clause_name: Rating Schedule-B - Nursing Home Excess Factors

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "Each million in limits is subject to a minimum premium of $1,000,000" is an evident error of magnitude — a minimum premium equal to the entire limit — most likely $1,000. The mistake changes the provision's meaning entirely.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It cannot be squared with the hospital minimum premium tables in the same schedule, where minimums run from $2,134 to $16,000 per million, nor with Article VI's premium mechanics.
judgments.clause_name: Rating Schedule-B - Nursing Home Minimum Premiums

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The factor is given as ".25" and the contingent endorsement charge as "258," figures that are internally inconsistent with the corresponding hospital entry (.125 and 25) and cannot be applied as written. The unit of each number is unstated.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The instruction applies the factor "to premium developed in OBE rating," yet nursing homes are rated off the reinsured's manual GL and PL premium, not off occupied bed equivalents, so the reference has no operative base.
judgments.clause_name: Rating Schedule-B - Nursing Home Indiana and Wisconsin Factor

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The base is the reinsured's own manual premium, an external and adjustable figure, and the automobile load for a private passenger vehicle appears as "$ 80.00" against $50.00 in the nursing home section without explanation. The 25% factor itself is clear.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It coordinates with the Facility excess factors and minimum premiums that follow, and with the outpatient facility coverage added by Amendment No. 4.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Rates per $1,000 of receipts are stated layer by layer with no soft terms, though "receipts" is not defined. The structure is otherwise mechanical.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The closing sentence routes automobile exposure back to the First Million rates and excess factors, which fits the preceding paragraphs.
judgments.clause_name: Rating Schedule-B - Facility Rating Imaging (MRI) Risks

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A capped discretionary credit, expressly excluded from minimum premiums. The wording is clear.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It refers to "OHIC's discretion" while the parallel nursing home provision says "the REINSURED'S discretion," a harmless variation given Amendment No. 3's name change.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Nine descending percentages paired with nine layers, each expressed as a percentage of the first million premium. Definite.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Consistent with the Facility minimum premium provision and with the $10,000,000 outpatient facility sub-limit in the amended Article III.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A first-million minimum premium of $1,500,000 and $1,000,000 per additional million are figures larger than or equal to the limits purchased, an obvious magnitude error (probably $1,500 and $1,000). As written the provision is unworkable.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It contradicts the hospital minimum premium tables in the same Schedule-B, where per-million minimums are in the thousands, and cannot be reconciled with Article VI's premium regime.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The factor is rendered ".is" rather than a number and the contingent endorsement charge as a bare "25," so the provision supplies no usable figure. That is a mechanical defect on its face.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Like the other Indiana/Wisconsin entries it applies a factor to "premium developed in OBE rating," which is not the basis on which facility business is rated in this section.
judgments.clause_name: Rating Schedule-B - Facility Indiana and Wisconsin Factor

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The stipulation terminates the treaty "with respect to loss under policies issued on or after January 1, 1998" without stating a termination date, and the phrase mixes a loss trigger with a policy-issuance trigger. It is unclear whether a "termination date" exists for the purposes of the articles that depend on one.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Article XI prescribes termination by mutual consent or 90 days' notice "stating the termination date," with run-off of in-force policies for up to twelve months plus odd time, and Article VII's contingent commission rules turn on that termination date; the stipulation's different formula leaves those mechanisms without a fixed trigger.
